**CHAPTER 1**   
**INTRODUCTION**

1.1  Background

Renting a residential property is one of the most common financial transactions in India. Millions of agreements are signed every year between landlords and tenants in cities, towns, and smaller localities across the country. Despite this enormous scale, the process through which most small landlords manage their properties has changed very little over the past two decades. A landlord finds a tenant, gets an agreement signed on printed paper, collects rent each month through informal channels, and handles maintenance issues over phone calls and messaging apps. The system works in simple, uncomplicated situations. But it begins to show cracks the moment anything needs to be verified, tracked, or disputed.

Most small landlords in India — individuals who own one to three residential units and let them out for income — are not using any software to manage their properties. They are using WhatsApp for communication, a physical register or a notes app for tracking payments, printed paper agreements for documentation, and their own memory for everything else. This arrangement is not the result of unwillingness to use technology. It is the result of a gap in the market. Property management software that exists today is either built for large-scale commercial landlords and property agencies, where the feature set is too complex and the pricing too high for a small landlord, or it is limited to basic digital ledgers that only track payments without addressing any of the other problems.

RentEase was built to fill this gap. It is a web-based application designed specifically for small residential landlords who manage one to three properties. The application brings together four things that currently exist in disconnected, informal places: rental agreements, payment records, maintenance complaints, and property and tenant information. All of this is accessible through a single browser-based interface, backed by a Firebase cloud database, and requires no installation, no technical knowledge, and no recurring cost to operate.

The project also includes a feature that distinguishes it from other simple property management tools: an AI-powered clause explainer built on the Google Gemini API. Rental agreements in India are typically written in dense legal language that many tenants and some landlords do not fully understand. The clause explainer allows any user to paste a section of their agreement and ask a question about it in plain language. The system returns a clear, grounded explanation based strictly on the pasted text. This feature was not part of the initial project concept — it emerged from a specific real-world problem that shaped the project from its earliest planning stages.

1.2  The Problem in Context

To understand the value of a system like RentEase, it is worth walking through what the actual experience of managing a small rental property typically involves. Consider a landlord who has two flats — a common scenario in Indian cities where individuals invest in residential property as supplementary income. When a new tenant moves in, the landlord either uses a printed template agreement purchased from a stationery shop, or visits a local notary who drafts one for a fee. The agreement is signed in two copies, one for each party. One copy gets filed somewhere — a drawer, a folder, a scanning app on the phone. The other copy goes home with the tenant, and in many cases is also put away and forgotten until needed.

After the first few months, tracking rent payments becomes the main ongoing task. Some landlords maintain a physical register. Others write notes in a mobile app or simply rely on their UPI transaction history to reconstruct who paid when. Neither approach gives a clean, reliable record. The UPI history shows that money was received, but not necessarily whether the correct amount was paid, whether it was on time, or whether there is any running dispute about it. A landlord managing two properties may have two different tenants on two different payment schedules, and keeping both sets of records accurate without a structured system requires constant attention.

Maintenance complaints are handled even more informally. A tenant sends a WhatsApp message at some point saying the water heater is malfunctioning. The landlord reads it, may or may not respond immediately, arranges for a repair at some point, or gets busy and lets it slide. There is no record of when the complaint was raised, whether it was assigned to a repair person, what the outcome was, or whether it was ever properly resolved. Weeks or months later, the tenant mentions it again, and neither party has a clear and shared account of what happened.

The rental agreement itself becomes a source of friction whenever a term needs to be verified. Both parties may interpret the same clause differently. Finding the original signed copy requires physical effort. Even when it is found, reading through the legal language requires careful attention, and the meaning of specific clauses — what exactly does the lock-in period provision say? what is the notice period? who is responsible for which maintenance? — is not always immediately clear to non-lawyers.

RentEase addresses all of these pain points in one integrated system. It does not replace every aspect of the landlord-tenant relationship — it still needs to be printed and signed to be legally binding, and payments still happen through whatever channels the parties agree on. What it does is digitize the documentation and tracking so that nothing gets lost, nothing gets forgotten, and nothing needs to be reconstructed from memory when a question arises.

1.3  Genesis of the Project

The idea for RentEase came from a real situation that one of the team members was close to. A family member who manages two flats had a dispute with a tenant about whether a lock-in period clause had been part of the original agreement. Neither party could find the signed copy quickly. The conversation about it dragged on for several days over something that should have been a straightforward five-minute lookup. When the team sat down to think about what a simple digital tool could have done to prevent or quickly resolve that dispute, they found themselves describing the core feature set of what became RentEase.

This project origin is important because it shaped the development priorities in a specific way. The team was not building a hypothetical solution to an imaginary problem. They had a concrete user in mind — a real person with a real property management situation — and they could check their design decisions against that person's actual workflow and constraints. This grounded the scope decisions, the UI choices, and the emphasis on simplicity throughout the development process.

The team also identified two technical learning goals that the project should serve. Neither member had used Firebase as a real backend for a multi-collection data model. They had followed tutorials, but had not built anything with properly linked data across multiple Firestore collections. They also wanted to integrate an AI API for the first time, which neither had done before. The clause explainer served as the concrete context for learning how to work with the Gemini API. These learning goals made RentEase not just a project submission but a genuine technical growth exercise.

1.4  Overview of the System

RentEase is organized around a single user type: the landlord. There is one login per landlord account. From the main dashboard, the landlord can navigate to any of the six core functional areas. The Property Management module handles the creation and management of property records. The Tenant Management module handles tenant profiles, including identity document uploads. The Agreement Generator produces downloadable rental agreements from a structured form. The Payment Tracker maintains a month-by-month payment log for each active tenant. The Maintenance Complaint module logs and tracks property maintenance issues. The AI Clause Explainer provides plain-language explanations of any pasted agreement clause.

All application data is stored in Firestore, organized across six collections: landlords, properties, tenants, agreements, payments, and complaints. Every document in every collection stores the landlord's Firebase Authentication UID as a field, which the security rules use to ensure that each landlord can only access their own data. Firebase Storage holds binary files — specifically, the identity document images that landlords upload when creating tenant profiles. The frontend is served from Firebase Hosting.

The application does not require installation. Any device with a modern web browser and an internet connection can access it. The responsive layout adapts to screens from mobile phones upward. The entire infrastructure runs within Firebase's free tier, which means there is no recurring cost for a deployment at the scale RentEase is designed for.

The following chapters describe the system in increasing levels of detail. Chapter 2 covers the objectives and scope. Chapter 3 covers the system analysis, including requirements specification. Chapter 4 covers the system design, including the architecture, DFDs, ER diagram, and database schema. Chapter 5 covers the user interface design. Chapter 6 covers the implementation details, code samples, and testing. Chapter 7 presents the conclusion, limitations, and future scope.

**CHAPTER 2**   
**OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE OF THE PROJECT**

2.1  Objectives of the System

The primary objective of RentEase is to replace the fragmented, manual approach that small residential landlords currently use to manage their rental properties with a single, integrated, and easy-to-use digital platform. This primary objective is decomposed into seven specific system objectives, each corresponding to a distinct functional module.

**Objective 1: Digital Agreement Generation**

The system shall allow a landlord to generate a complete, formatted rental agreement by filling in a structured form. The form shall collect all the standard information required in a residential rental agreement: the full names and addresses of both parties, the complete property address, the monthly rent amount, the security deposit amount, the agreement start date, the lock-in period duration, the notice period duration, and the basic maintenance responsibilities. The resulting agreement shall be downloadable as a PDF file from the browser without any server-side processing.

**Objective 2: Tenant Profile Management**

The system shall provide a structured digital profile for each tenant. The profile shall store all relevant personal and tenancy information: full name, phone number, email address, move-in date, and the identity document number with the option to upload a scanned copy. The profile shall also link to the tenant's agreement record and payment history, creating a single place where all information related to a tenancy is accessible.

**Objective 3: Monthly Rent Tracking**

The system shall provide a month-by-month payment tracker for each tenant, beginning from their move-in date and extending to the current month. The landlord shall be able to mark each month as paid, pending, or partially paid, add a note, and record the date of payment. The tracker shall display the complete payment history at a glance, making it easy to identify overdue months without needing to search through messages or call records.

**Objective 4: Automated Rent Reminders**

The system shall send an automated notification to the landlord when a tenant's rent due date is approaching. The landlord shall be able to configure both the due date for each tenant and the number of advance days for the reminder. This removes the need for the landlord to remember to send reminders manually and reduces the awkwardness of what many landlords experience as an uncomfortable monthly message.

**Objective 5: Maintenance Complaint Logging**

The system shall provide a structured interface for logging and tracking property maintenance complaints. Each complaint record shall include a description of the issue, a category (plumbing, electrical, structural, or other), a priority level (low, medium, or high), the date the complaint was raised, the current status (open, in progress, or resolved), and a resolution note that the landlord can update as the issue is addressed. The complaint log provides a clear chronological record for both parties.

**Objective 6: AI Clause Explainer**

The system shall provide a text interface where a landlord or tenant can paste any section of a rental agreement and ask a question about it in plain language. The system shall pass the pasted text and the question to the Google Gemini API with a structured prompt that constrains the response to the provided text only, and shall display the returned explanation in clear, readable language. This feature addresses one of the most practically significant problems in rental relationships: the gap between the legal language of written agreements and what both parties actually understand them to mean.

**Objective 7: Unified Property Dashboard**

The system shall provide a single overview dashboard showing all of the landlord's properties, the current tenant at each property, the payment status for the current month, and the count of open maintenance complaints. The dashboard shall give the landlord a complete picture of their rental portfolio in a single view, without requiring navigation to individual property pages for a status overview.

2.2  Scope of the Project

The scope of RentEase is deliberately defined to be achievable within the project timeline while still delivering genuine value. The scope boundary was drawn based on three criteria: whether the feature addresses a problem that the target user actually has, whether the feature is implementable within the available time and skills, and whether the feature is genuinely necessary for the core use case or can be deferred to a future version.

Within scope for the current version: a single landlord account per installation; management of up to five residential properties (with no hard technical limit); one active tenant per property at any given time with historical records retained; standard residential rental agreement generation in English; month-by-month payment tracking for monthly rent; maintenance complaint logging and status tracking; an AI clause explainer powered by the Gemini API; and a responsive web interface accessible from any modern browser.

Explicitly outside scope for the current version: a tenant-facing login portal; a payment gateway or any integration with banking or UPI systems; legally stamped or electronically signed agreements; leave-and-licence agreement templates (as distinct from standard rental agreements); commercial property management; management of utility payments, maintenance expenses, or other financial transactions; multi-user accounts or property management agency features; and offline functionality.

The decision to exclude a tenant portal was the most debated scope decision. Having tenants log in to see their own agreement, track their payments, and raise complaints directly would significantly increase the value of the system for tenants. However, it would also roughly double the development complexity: a separate user role, separate data views, separate notification flows, and separate security rules. Given the project timeline and the team's technical level at the time, this was deferred to future scope and is discussed in Chapter 7\.

2.3  Target Users

The system is designed for a specific and well-defined primary user: an individual landlord who owns one to three residential properties in India and currently manages them using informal digital tools and paper documents. This user is not a technical professional. They are comfortable with smartphones and basic web applications, but they have not used property management software before. They do not want to learn a complex interface. They want something that works like a well-organized folder combined with a simple form-based input system.

Secondary users, who are represented in the system but do not have their own login, are the tenants. In the current version, tenants interact with RentEase indirectly — through the agreements generated for them, through the payment records maintained by the landlord, and through the complaints that the landlord logs on their behalf. In a future version with a tenant portal, they would become direct users of the system.

The system also has an implied secondary beneficiary: the landlord's tenants, even without a login. When a landlord uses RentEase, their tenants benefit because there is now a clear, retrievable record of their agreement, a transparent payment history, and a tracked complaint log. The system's value is not limited to the person who logs in.

2.4  System Boundaries and Assumptions

Several boundaries and assumptions are important to state clearly for anyone evaluating or deploying RentEase. First, the system is a record-keeping and documentation tool. It does not collect money. When a payment is marked as paid, that means the landlord has received money through some channel — UPI, bank transfer, cash — and has recorded it in the system. The system does not facilitate or verify the transaction.

Second, the agreement generated by RentEase is a formatted template, not a legally stamped document. For the agreement to have legal standing in a dispute, it must be printed, signed by both parties, and ideally registered as required by local law. The system does not handle any of these post-generation steps. This limitation is explicitly disclosed in the interface and is described in detail in the limitations section of Chapter 7\.

Third, the AI clause explainer is an explanatory tool, not a legal advice service. The responses it provides are based on the text pasted by the user and are intended to help that user understand what a clause says in plain language. They do not constitute a legal opinion, do not assess the enforceability of any clause, and should not be used as a substitute for proper legal counsel in a serious dispute. A disclaimer to this effect is permanently displayed on the AI explainer page.

The system assumes that all users have access to a device with a modern web browser and a reasonably stable internet connection. It assumes that identity document uploads are made in good faith and that the landlord takes responsibility for the accuracy of the information entered. The system does not perform identity verification of any kind.

**CHAPTER 3**   
**SYSTEM ANALYSIS**

3.1  Analysis of the Existing System

Before any design work began, the team conducted an analysis of how the target users currently manage their properties. The primary source was a series of structured conversations with the individual whose experience had inspired the project, supplemented by the team's own observation of how property management typically works in their social and family contexts.

The existing approach among small landlords involves at minimum three or four separate tools that were not designed to work together. The rental agreement is a physical paper document, either a generic template or a notary-drafted copy. Payment tracking happens in a personal notes application, a physical register, or is reconstructed from UPI history when needed. Maintenance issues are communicated and discussed entirely through WhatsApp or phone calls. Tenant contact information is stored in the phone's contact list, mixed in with hundreds of other contacts.

None of these tools communicate with each other. If a landlord wants to answer the question 'how many months has the tenant in Flat 2 been late on rent over the past year?', they need to go through their UPI history month by month, correlate it against whatever record they kept, and manually count. If they want to check whether the current tenant's agreement includes a clause about who pays for minor plumbing repairs, they need to physically find the signed agreement and read through it. These tasks are not impossible. They are just time-consuming and error-prone in ways that a digital system can eliminate.

The team also installed and evaluated two commercial property management applications available for Android during the analysis phase. Both applications were oriented towards larger-scale property managers and offered features like commission tracking, bulk invoicing, agent management, and multi-user dashboards. Neither offered agreement generation. Neither had an AI feature. Both required either a subscription or a large enough portfolio to justify the interface complexity. They confirmed the gap in the market that RentEase was designed to fill.

3.2  Limitations of the Existing Approach

The limitations of the current informal approach to property management can be grouped into five categories, each of which corresponds directly to a feature of RentEase.

**Document Management Limitations**

Paper agreements are vulnerable in ways that digital records are not. They can be lost in a move, damaged by water or fire, or simply misplaced over the years of a tenancy. Even landlords who photograph or scan their agreements often store the images in a personal cloud drive without any organizational structure — the image of one agreement looks the same as any other in a folder full of photos. When a clause needs to be checked, finding the relevant document takes effort. RentEase solves this by generating and storing a structured record of every agreement, indexed by tenant and property, accessible in seconds.

**Payment Tracking Limitations**

Without a structured tracking system, payment records are unreliable. UPI history provides a timestamp and an amount but no context. A record showing that Rs. 18,500 was received on the 12th of March does not automatically indicate which tenant it was for, whether it was for March or a make-up for February, whether any penalty was applied for lateness, or whether there was a dispute about the amount. Physical registers are more structured but can only be maintained by someone who is disciplined about updating them consistently, which many landlords are not. RentEase provides a month-by-month tracker that requires only a click to update, with a notes field for any contextual information.

**Maintenance Tracking Limitations**

Maintenance complaints sent via WhatsApp have no structure, no priority level, no assignment, and no formal tracking. The same message thread contains informal conversation, maintenance requests, and rent discussions all mixed together. Whether a specific complaint was ever resolved requires going back through the chat history and looking for a resolution message — and sometimes there is none because the issue was resolved verbally, on a call, without any message. RentEase provides a separate complaint log with explicit status tracking so that every logged issue has a clear state at any point in time.

**Communication Limitations**

Many landlords report feeling awkward about sending rent reminders. This leads to inconsistent reminder behavior — some months the landlord sends a reminder, some months they do not, and the pattern is determined by mood and memory rather than any consistent system. When reminders are not sent, tenants who would have paid on time if reminded sometimes pay late, and the resulting conversation can be uncomfortable for both parties. An automated reminder system removes this entirely by making the reminder a system function rather than a personal communication.

**Agreement Comprehension Limitations**

The language used in rental agreements in India is typically derived from standard legal templates. Clauses about lock-in periods, notice periods, maintenance responsibilities, and dispute resolution are written in a style that is technically precise but not easy for non-lawyers to parse at a glance. The practical consequence is that many tenants sign agreements without fully understanding all of the terms, and disputes arise because both parties had different understandings of what a clause meant. The AI clause explainer addresses this directly by making plain-language explanation of any clause instantly available without requiring either party to call a lawyer or attempt to interpret legal language themselves.

3.3  Feasibility Study

**Technical Feasibility**

All the technologies used in RentEase are freely available, well-documented, and actively maintained. Firebase is one of the most widely deployed Backend-as-a-Service platforms in the world, with comprehensive documentation and a large developer community. The Gemini API is part of Google's AI developer platform and provides a straightforward REST interface for making generative AI calls. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap 5 are foundational web technologies with decades of accumulated documentation. The team assessed the technical feasibility as high, with the acknowledgment that the AI integration specifically would require more experimentation and iteration than the other components. This assessment proved accurate — the Gemini API integration required approximately nine or ten prompt iterations before producing reliably useful responses.

**Operational Feasibility**

Operational feasibility asks whether the intended users will actually be able to use the system effectively. RentEase was designed from the beginning with a non-technical primary user in mind. The interface uses familiar web conventions — forms, buttons, tables, modals — that do not require any training to understand. The core workflow (add a property, add a tenant, generate an agreement, track a payment) was tested with users unfamiliar with the system, and both test participants completed it successfully within fifteen minutes without assistance. The operational feasibility was assessed as high.

**Economic Feasibility**

The entire system runs on the Firebase free tier, which provides 1 GB of Firestore storage, 10 GB of Firebase Hosting bandwidth per month, 50,000 daily active users for authentication, and 5 GB of Firebase Storage. For a single-landlord deployment managing a handful of properties, these limits are effectively unlimited. Development cost is measured in time, not money. No licensing fees, hosting fees, or per-user charges apply. Economic feasibility was assessed as not a constraint.

3.4  Functional Requirements

The functional requirements specify what the system must do. Each requirement is labeled with an identifier for cross-referencing in the test case table in Chapter 6\.

FR-01: The system shall allow a new user to create an account using an email address and password. The email must be unique across all accounts. Password validation shall enforce a minimum length of six characters.

FR-02: The system shall authenticate a registered user using their email and password. On successful authentication, the system shall establish a session and redirect the user to the dashboard. On failed authentication, the system shall display a specific error message identifying the reason for failure.

FR-03: The system shall allow an authenticated landlord to create a property record. The record shall include property name, complete address, property type, number of rooms, and monthly rent amount.

FR-04: The system shall allow an authenticated landlord to view, edit, and delete their property records. Editing shall update the stored record. Deletion shall be preceded by a confirmation dialog and shall cascade to update the occupancy status.

FR-05: The system shall allow an authenticated landlord to create a tenant profile linked to a specific property. The profile shall include full name, phone number, email address, move-in date, and an optional identity document upload.

FR-06: The system shall provide an agreement generation form that collects landlord details, tenant details, property address, and agreement terms. On submission, the form shall produce a downloadable formatted PDF agreement.

FR-07: The system shall maintain a month-by-month payment tracker for each active tenant, beginning from their move-in date. The landlord shall be able to update the payment status for any month.

FR-08: The system shall allow an authenticated landlord to create maintenance complaint records linked to a property. Each record shall include description, category, priority, and date. The landlord shall be able to update the status of any complaint.

FR-09: The system shall provide an AI clause explainer interface that accepts pasted agreement text and a plain-language question, calls the Gemini API, and displays the response.

FR-10: The system shall display a dashboard summarizing all properties, active tenants, current month payment status, and open complaint counts.

3.5  Non-Functional Requirements

Non-functional requirements describe the quality attributes of the system — how it performs, how secure it is, how usable it is — rather than what it does.

NFR-01 (Performance): All pages shall load within three seconds on a standard broadband internet connection. Firestore read operations on collections with fewer than one hundred documents shall complete within one second.

NFR-02 (Usability): A new user with no prior experience of the system shall be able to complete the core workflow — add a property, add a tenant, and generate an agreement — within fifteen minutes of first login, without consulting any documentation.

NFR-03 (Security): All data access shall be protected by Firestore security rules. Each landlord shall only be able to read and write their own data. Unauthenticated requests shall be denied for all read and write operations.

NFR-04 (Reliability): The system shall run on Firebase's managed infrastructure, which provides 99.95% uptime. No additional reliability engineering is required at the application level for the current deployment scale.

NFR-05 (Responsiveness): The system shall display and function correctly on screen widths from 320 pixels upward, covering mobile phones, tablets, and desktop displays.

NFR-06 (Maintainability): JavaScript modules shall have clear, descriptive names. Functions shall include comments explaining their purpose. The Firestore data structure shall be documented so that it can be understood without reference to the application code.

NFR-07 (Portability): The application shall run on any modern web browser without requiring plugins, extensions, or special configurations. It shall not rely on any browser-specific API that is not available in all major browsers.

**CHAPTER 4**   
**SYSTEM DESIGN**

4.1  System Architecture

RentEase follows a three-tier web architecture in which the three tiers are the presentation tier, the logic tier, and the data tier. What makes this architecture slightly non-traditional is the absence of a custom application server in the logic tier — Firebase's managed services fill that role entirely.

The presentation tier consists of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files that run inside the user's web browser. Bootstrap 5 provides the responsive grid layout and pre-built UI components. Vanilla JavaScript handles all client-side logic: event handling, form validation, DOM updates, Firebase SDK calls, and Gemini API requests. No JavaScript framework was used. The decision to avoid React or Vue was deliberate — neither team member had enough experience with these frameworks to use them confidently under time pressure, and plain JavaScript turned out to be entirely sufficient for the application's requirements.

The logic tier is provided by Firebase's suite of services. Firebase Authentication handles user registration, login, session management, and logout. The Firebase JavaScript SDK provides method-level abstractions over the Firestore REST API, so the client code calls named functions rather than constructing raw HTTP requests. Firestore's real-time listeners allow certain views — such as the dashboard — to update automatically when underlying data changes without the user needing to refresh the page.

The data tier consists of Firestore for all structured application data and Firebase Storage for binary file uploads. Firestore organizes data as collections of JSON-like documents, each identified by a unique auto-generated ID. Firebase Storage organizes files under configurable path prefixes. Firestore Security Rules, which run server-side in Firebase's infrastructure, enforce data access control for all read and write operations.

One important characteristic of this architecture is that all business logic runs in the client-side JavaScript. There is no custom backend server processing requests. This means that the security of the application depends entirely on the Firestore Security Rules being correct and complete — because client-side code is always visible to users with browser developer tools, any logic that must not be bypassed must be enforced in the security rules, not in the application code. The team addressed this by testing the security rules specifically as part of the testing phase described in Chapter 6\.

4.2  Data Flow Diagram – Level 0 (Context Diagram)

The Context Diagram represents the complete RentEase system as a single central process and identifies the external entities that interact with it. At this level of abstraction, the internal structure of the system is not shown — only the inputs and outputs that cross the system boundary.

Five external entities are identified. The Landlord is the primary user who provides inputs — credentials, property data, tenant data, agreement information, payment updates, complaint records, and pasted clause text — and receives outputs — authenticated sessions, data views, generated agreements, payment histories, AI explanations, and the dashboard summary.

Firebase Authentication is an external service that receives authentication requests (create account, sign in, sign out) and returns authentication responses (user credential objects, session tokens, or error codes). Firestore is an external data service that receives structured read and write requests and returns document data or confirmation responses. Firebase Storage is an external file service that receives file upload requests and returns download URLs. The Gemini API is an external AI service that receives structured prompt requests containing clause text and user questions, and returns plain-language text responses.

*Figure 4.2 DFD Level 0*

![][image2]

4.3  Data Flow Diagram – Level 1

The Level 1 DFD decomposes the single RentEase process into its six major sub-processes, revealing the internal structure of the system and how data flows between the modules and the external data stores.

Process 1 – User Authentication: Receives login credentials from the Landlord entity and communicates with Firebase Authentication (D0 – Auth Store). On success, returns a session containing the landlord's UID, which is passed to all other processes as a scope key. Writes a landlord profile document to D1 (Landlords Collection) on first registration.

Process 2 – Property Management: Receives property information from the Landlord, performs CRUD operations on D2 (Properties Collection), and returns property lists for display on the dashboard and property management page. Updates the isOccupied flag when a tenant is added or removed from a property.

Process 3 – Tenant Management: Receives tenant profile information from the Landlord, writes profile data to D3 (Tenants Collection), and uploads identity documents to D7 (Firebase Storage). Reads D2 to validate that the linked property exists and belongs to the current landlord. Returns tenant profiles for display.

Process 4 – Agreement Generation: Reads property and tenant data from D2 and D3 to pre-populate form fields. Receives additional agreement terms from the Landlord form input. Generates a PDF document client-side and sends it directly to the Landlord as a file download. Writes an agreement summary record to D4 (Agreements Collection).

Process 5 – Payment and Complaint Tracking: Receives payment status updates from the Landlord and writes them to D5 (Payments Collection). Receives complaint submissions and status updates from the Landlord and reads/writes D6 (Complaints Collection). Returns payment history and complaint logs for display.

Process 6 – AI Clause Explainer: Receives pasted clause text and a question from the Landlord. Constructs a structured prompt and sends it to the Gemini API (External Service D8). Returns the AI-generated explanation to the Landlord for display on the explainer page.

*Figure 4.3 DFD Level 1* 

![][image3]

4.4  Data Flow Diagram – Level 2 (Agreement Generation)

The Level 2 DFD for Process 4 (Agreement Generation) provides additional detail on the internal sub-steps within the agreement generation flow, which is the most complex single process in the system.

Sub-process 4.1 – Form Validation: The Landlord submits the agreement generation form. Client-side JavaScript validates each field: required fields must not be empty, the rent amount must be a positive number, date fields must be valid, and period lengths (lock-in and notice) must be positive integers. If validation fails, the process stops and error messages are displayed inline.

Sub-process 4.2 – Data Enrichment: The validated form data is enriched with property and tenant details fetched from Firestore (D2 and D3). This ensures that the agreement uses the stored property address and tenant name from the database rather than whatever was typed in the form, preventing discrepancies between the stored records and the generated document.

Sub-process 4.3 – Template Population: The enriched data is merged into the agreement template. The template is an HTML string with named placeholder variables (e.g., {{TENANT\_NAME}}, {{PROPERTY\_ADDRESS}}, {{MONTHLY\_RENT}}). A JavaScript function iterates over the placeholders and substitutes each one with the corresponding data value.

Sub-process 4.4 – PDF Generation and Storage: The populated HTML template is passed to jsPDF, which renders it as a formatted PDF and triggers a browser download. Simultaneously, a summary record is written to D4 (Agreements Collection) capturing the key terms without storing the full agreement text.

*Figure 4.4 DFD Level 2 (Agreement Generation)* 

![][image4]

4.5  Entity-Relationship Diagram

The ER Diagram defines the complete data model of RentEase. Six entities are identified, along with their attributes and the relationships between them.

The Landlord entity is the root of all data in the system. Every other entity traces back to a landlord through its landlordId field. Attributes: landlordId (PK, Firebase Auth UID), displayName, email, createdAt.

The Property entity represents one residential unit. Attributes: propertyId (PK, auto), landlordId (FK → Landlord), propertyName, address, type (apartment/house/flat/studio), numberOfRooms, monthlyRent, isOccupied (boolean), createdAt.

The Tenant entity represents one active or historical tenant. Attributes: tenantId (PK, auto), propertyId (FK → Property), landlordId (FK → Landlord), fullName, phoneNumber, email, identityDocUrl, moveInDate, isActive (boolean), createdAt.

The Agreement entity represents a generated agreement document. Attributes: agreementId (PK, auto), tenantId (FK → Tenant), propertyId (FK → Property), landlordId (FK → Landlord), startDate, lockInPeriod, noticePeriod, monthlyRent, securityDeposit, generatedAt.

The Payment entity represents one monthly payment record. Attributes: paymentId (composite: tenantId\_YYYY-MM), tenantId (FK → Tenant), landlordId (FK → Landlord), month (YYYY-MM), status (paid/pending/partial), paidOn, amount, notes.

The Complaint entity represents one maintenance complaint. Attributes: complaintId (PK, auto), propertyId (FK → Property), landlordId (FK → Landlord), description, category, priority, dateRaised, status (open/in-progress/resolved), resolutionNote.

Relationships: A Landlord manages many Properties (one-to-many). A Property has one currently active Tenant and many historical Tenants (one-to-many). A Tenant has at most one active Agreement (one-to-one in practice). A Tenant has many Payment records (one-to-many). A Property has many Complaints (one-to-many).

*Figure 4.5 Entity-Relationship Diagram* 

![][image5]

4.6  Database Design

The Firestore database for RentEase uses a flat collection structure — all six collections are at the top level, with relationships expressed through stored foreign-key fields rather than Firestore subcollections. This approach simplifies querying (each collection can be queried independently with a where clause) and simplifies security rules (each collection has one simple ownership rule).

**Table 4.1 – Firestore Collections Overview**

| Collection Name | Purpose | Primary Key | Ownership Field |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| landlords | Stores landlord profile documents | Firebase Auth UID (set as document ID) | Document ID \== landlordId |
| properties | Stores property records | Auto-generated Firestore ID | landlordId |
| tenants | Stores tenant profiles | Auto-generated Firestore ID | landlordId |
| agreements | Stores agreement summary records | Auto-generated Firestore ID | landlordId |
| payments | Stores monthly payment records | Composite: tenantId\_YYYY-MM | landlordId |
| complaints | Stores maintenance complaint records | Auto-generated Firestore ID | landlordId |

**Table 4.2 – 'landlords' Collection Schema**

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| landlordId | String (document ID) | Firebase Auth UID; used as document ID and primary key across all collections |
| displayName | String | Full name of the landlord as entered during registration |
| email | String | Email address used for login and correspondence |
| createdAt | Timestamp | Server-generated timestamp of account creation |

**Table 4.3 – 'properties' Collection Schema**

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| propertyId | String (auto) | Auto-generated Firestore document ID |
| landlordId | String (ref) | UID of the owning landlord; used in security rules |
| propertyName | String | Short name for the property (e.g., 'Flat 3B, Building A') |
| address | String | Complete postal address |
| type | String (enum) | apartment / house / flat / studio |
| numberOfRooms | Number | Total number of rooms (bedrooms \+ common areas) |
| monthlyRent | Number | Standard monthly rent amount in INR |
| isOccupied | Boolean | True if a tenant is currently active at this property |
| createdAt | Timestamp | Server-generated timestamp of record creation |

**Table 4.4 – 'tenants' Collection Schema**

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| tenantId | String (auto) | Auto-generated Firestore document ID |
| landlordId | String (ref) | UID of the owning landlord |
| propertyId | String (ref) | Document ID of the linked property |
| fullName | String | Tenant's full name |
| phoneNumber | String | Primary contact phone number |
| email | String | Tenant's email address |
| identityDocUrl | String | Firebase Storage download URL for the uploaded ID document |
| moveInDate | String (ISO date) | Date the tenant moved in; used as start of payment tracker range |
| isActive | Boolean | True if the tenant is currently active at the property |
| createdAt | Timestamp | Record creation timestamp |

**Table 4.5 – 'payments' Collection Schema**

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| paymentId | String (composite) | Manually set as 'tenantId\_YYYY-MM' for deterministic lookup |
| landlordId | String (ref) | UID of the owning landlord |
| tenantId | String (ref) | Reference to the tenant document |
| month | String (YYYY-MM) | The calendar month this record represents |
| status | String (enum) | paid / pending / partial |
| amount | Number (nullable) | Amount actually received (null if pending) |
| paidOn | String (ISO date, nullable) | Date payment was received |
| notes | String | Optional notes (e.g., 'Partial — Rs 5000 short, balance next month') |

**Table 4.6 – 'complaints' Collection Schema**

| Field Name | Data Type | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| complaintId | String (auto) | Auto-generated Firestore document ID |
| landlordId | String (ref) | UID of the owning landlord |
| propertyId | String (ref) | Reference to the property where the complaint was raised |
| description | String | Full description of the maintenance issue |
| category | String (enum) | plumbing / electrical / structural / other |
| priority | String (enum) | low / medium / high |
| dateRaised | String (ISO date) | Date the complaint was logged |
| status | String (enum) | open / in-progress / resolved |
| resolutionNote | String | Description of how the issue was resolved (optional until resolved) |

4.7  System Planning – PERT Chart

The development timeline for RentEase spanned approximately twelve weeks. Activities were identified, their durations estimated, and their dependencies mapped to produce a PERT network. The following table describes each activity and its dependency.

| Activity | Description | Duration (weeks) | Depends On |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| A | Requirements gathering, problem definition, user interviews | 1.5 | — |
| B | Firestore schema design and Firebase project setup | 1 | A |
| C | UI wireframing (paper sketches for five main screens) | 0.5 | A |
| D | Authentication module: registration, login, session handling | 1 | B |
| E | Property management module: CRUD for property records | 1 | D |
| F | Tenant management module: profiles and document upload | 1 | E |
| G | Agreement generator: form, template, PDF output | 1.5 | F |
| H | Payment tracker: month range generation, status tracking | 1 | F |
| I | Maintenance complaint module: log and status update | 0.5 | F |
| J | AI clause explainer: Gemini API integration and prompt tuning | 1 | D |
| K | Dashboard integration: aggregate stats from all modules | 0.5 | G, H, I |
| L | Integration testing: end-to-end workflow testing | 1 | K, J |
| M | Usability testing with external participants and bug fixing | 0.5 | L |
| N | Final deployment to Firebase Hosting | 0.5 | M |
| O | Documentation and report writing | 1 | N |

Critical Path: A → B → D → F → G → K → L → M → N → O (approximately 10.5 weeks). Activities C, E, H, I, and J run in parallel with activities on the critical path and do not extend the overall project duration if completed within their respective windows.

**CHAPTER 5**   
**USER INTERFACE DESIGN**

5.1  Design Principles

The user interface of RentEase was designed around one guiding principle: the primary user is a non-technical individual who has never used property management software. Every design decision was evaluated against this principle. Choices that made the interface more capable but harder to understand were avoided. Choices that simplified the interface even at the cost of advanced features were favored.

Five specific principles informed the detailed design work. The first principle was clarity over convention. Interface elements are labeled with exactly what they do. Buttons say 'Add Property', 'Mark as Paid', 'Submit Complaint' rather than icons alone or abstract labels. Navigation items describe their destination rather than using clever names. Where terminology might be ambiguous, the clearer term was chosen over the more technically correct one.

The second principle was progressive disclosure. Each screen shows only the information relevant to the task at hand. Detailed records — the full tenant profile, the complete payment history, the full complaint log — are accessed through a click rather than displayed by default. The dashboard shows summaries. The detail pages show records. The user is never confronted with more information than they need for their current task.

The third principle was immediate and specific feedback. Every action produces a visible response within one second. Successful form submissions show a green toast notification specifying what was saved. Failed operations show a red notification specifying what went wrong. Loading states are shown for any operation that takes more than 300 milliseconds. The user is never in a situation where they do not know whether their action was registered.

The fourth principle was error prevention over error messages. Required fields are marked visually and validated before submission is allowed. Destructive actions — deleting a property record, removing a tenant profile — require explicit confirmation through a modal dialog. The submit button on forms is disabled while a submission is in progress to prevent duplicate submissions. Where possible, the user is prevented from making mistakes rather than informed of them after the fact.

The fifth principle was mobile-first layout. The primary use case for many features — marking a payment received, checking a complaint status, looking up a tenant's phone number — is more likely to happen on a mobile phone than on a laptop. The layout was designed to work correctly at 375 pixels wide and then adapted for larger screens. Bootstrap 5's responsive grid system handles the majority of the layout adaptation automatically.

5.2  Color Scheme and Typography

The color scheme uses a restrained palette of four main colors. The primary color is a medium blue (\#1565C0), used for primary buttons, active navigation items, and section headings. The secondary color is a dark grey-blue (\#263238), used for the navigation bar background and heavy text elements. The accent color is a forest green (\#2E7D32), used for success states, paid payment badges, and positive indicators. A warm orange (\#E65100) is used for warning states, pending payment badges, and medium-priority complaint indicators.

Typography uses Bootstrap's default type scale throughout. Page headings are 24–28px. Section headings are 18–20px. Body text is 16px with 1.5 line height. All text is set in the system's default sans-serif stack (Bootstrap's native font stack), which renders as San Francisco on Apple devices, Segoe UI on Windows, and the Roboto/Noto family on Android. This choice was made for compatibility and load performance rather than brand distinction.

5.3  Screen Descriptions

**Screen 1: Login and Registration**

The login page is the entry point for all users. It displays a centered card with the RentEase logotype at the top, an email input, a password input, and a Login button. Below the button are two text links: 'New user? Create account' and 'Forgot password?'. The card is set to a maximum width of 440 pixels and is horizontally centered on all screen sizes. The background uses a subtle geometric pattern in muted blue to provide visual interest without distraction.

The registration page uses the same card layout and adds a single additional field: the user's full name. There is no role selection because all users in the current version are landlords. Client-side validation checks that the name field is not empty, the email is correctly formatted, and the password is at least six characters. If validation fails, red error text appears below the relevant field. Firebase Auth error responses — such as 'email already in use' — are mapped to plain-language messages and shown in a red alert box above the form.

Each card has a colored icon, the number in large text, and a label.

Below the metric cards is a 'My Properties' section showing property cards in a responsive grid. Each card displays the property name, address, type badge, monthly rent, and occupancy status. Two quick-action links at the bottom of each card navigate to 'View Tenants' and 'View Complaints' for that property.

The Property Management page shows all properties in a table with columns for Property Name, Address, Type, Monthly Rent, Status (Occupied/Vacant), and Actions. The Tenant Management page for a specific property shows the current tenant's profile. If no tenant is currently active, a prompt to add a tenant is displayed. Below the summary is the identity document section: if a document has been uploaded, a thumbnail link is shown. If not, an upload button is shown.

The Agreement Generator is a multi-section form divided into three visual sections separated by horizontal dividers. Section 1 – 'Party Details' collects the landlord's name and address and the tenant's name and current address. Section 3 – 'Agreement Terms' collects the monthly rent amount, security deposit amount, agreement start date, lock-in period in months, notice period in months, and rent due date (day of the month).

**CHAPTER 6**   
**SYSTEM IMPLEMENTATION AND TESTING**

6.1  Development Methodology

The development of RentEase followed a phased, sequential approach. Four phases were defined before development began: requirements and planning, database and architecture design, module development, and testing and deployment. Each phase had to be substantially complete before the next began. Within each phase, there was room for iteration — redesigning a form layout, reworking a Firestore query, revising a Gemini prompt — but the overall progression was linear.

The team divided responsibilities based on interest and complementary skills. Yuvraj took ownership of the frontend — all HTML pages, CSS styling, Bootstrap component configuration, and the UI layout for every screen. Raghav took ownership of the backend and integration layers — Firebase project setup, Firestore collection structure, JavaScript logic for database operations, Gemini API integration, security rules, and deployment.

Version control was managed through GitHub with a shared repository. The team followed a simple branching rule: each major feature was developed on a named branch (e.g., feature/agreement-generator, feature/payment-tracker), and branches were merged to main only when the feature was tested and working. This prevented partially completed features from destabilizing the working state of the main branch and made it straightforward to identify when a specific problem was introduced.

Claude AI and GitHub Copilot were used throughout development as coding assistants. They were particularly valuable in three areas: Firestore security rules (which have a domain-specific syntax not covered in most general web development tutorials), Gemini API prompt design (where multiple iterations were needed before the output was reliably useful), and the jsPDF layout logic for the agreement generator (where the coordinate-based drawing API requires familiarity with its specific dimensions system). The team treated AI suggestions as a starting point for understanding rather than as copy-paste solutions — every suggested piece of code was read, understood, and adapted before use.

6.2  Technology Stack Details

**6.2.1 Firebase Configuration**

The Firebase project for RentEase was initialized using the Firebase CLI. The firebase init command sets up the project directory with configuration files for the services being used: Firestore (firestore.rules, firestore.indexes.json), Firebase Hosting (firebase.json with routing configuration), and Firebase Storage (storage.rules). The Firebase configuration object — containing the project's API key, auth domain, and other identifiers — is stored in a dedicated firebase-config.js file that is imported by all other modules.

// firebase-config.js  
import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app';  
import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth';  
import { getFirestore } from 'firebase/firestore';  
import { getStorage } from 'firebase/storage';

const firebaseConfig \= {  
  apiKey: 'YOUR\_API\_KEY',  
  authDomain: 'rentease-app.firebaseapp.com',  
  projectId: 'rentease-app',  
  storageBucket: 'rentease-app.appspot.com',  
  messagingSenderId: 'YOUR\_SENDER\_ID',  
  appId: 'YOUR\_APP\_ID'  
};

const app \= initializeApp(firebaseConfig);  
export const auth \= getAuth(app);  
export const db \= getFirestore(app);  
export const storage \= getStorage(app);

**6.2.2 Authentication Module**

The authentication module handles user registration, login, and session management. All Firebase Auth method calls are wrapped in try-catch blocks and return a standardized result object containing a success boolean, relevant data on success, or a user-friendly error message on failure. Firebase Auth error codes are mapped to plain-language messages to avoid exposing technical error strings in the UI.

// auth.js  
import { auth, db } from './firebase-config.js';  
import {  
  createUserWithEmailAndPassword,  
  signInWithEmailAndPassword,  
  signOut,  
  onAuthStateChanged  
} from 'firebase/auth';  
import { doc, setDoc, serverTimestamp } from 'firebase/firestore';

// Register a new landlord account  
async function registerLandlord(email, password, displayName) {  
  try {  
    const cred \= await createUserWithEmailAndPassword(auth, email, password);  
    const uid  \= cred.user.uid;  
    await setDoc(doc(db, 'landlords', uid), {  
      landlordId:  uid,  
      displayName: displayName,  
      email:       email,  
      createdAt:   serverTimestamp()  
    });  
    return { success: true, uid };  
  } catch (err) {  
    return { success: false, error: mapAuthError(err.code) };  
  }  
}

// Map Firebase error codes to readable messages  
function mapAuthError(code) {  
  const map \= {  
    'auth/user-not-found':     'No account exists with this email address.',  
    'auth/wrong-password':     'The password you entered is incorrect.',  
    'auth/email-already-in-use': 'An account with this email already exists.',  
    'auth/weak-password':      'Password must be at least 6 characters.',  
    'auth/too-many-requests':  'Too many failed attempts. Please try again later.'  
  };  
  return map\[code\] || 'Something went wrong. Please try again.';  
}

// Observe session changes — call on every page load  
function observeAuthState(onLoggedIn, onLoggedOut) {  
  onAuthStateChanged(auth, user \=\> {  
    user ? onLoggedIn(user) : onLoggedOut();  
  });  
}

export { registerLandlord, observeAuthState };

**6.2.3 Property Management Module**

The property management module provides the full set of CRUD operations for property records. The subscribeToProperties function uses Firestore's real-time onSnapshot listener rather than a one-time getDocs call, so the property list on the UI updates automatically whenever any property is added, edited, or deleted without requiring a page refresh.

// properties.js  
import { db } from './firebase-config.js';  
import {  
  collection, doc, addDoc, updateDoc, deleteDoc,  
  query, where, orderBy, onSnapshot, serverTimestamp  
} from 'firebase/firestore';

// Add a new property record  
async function addProperty(landlordId, data) {  
  try {  
    const ref \= await addDoc(collection(db, 'properties'), {  
      landlordId:    landlordId,  
      propertyName:  data.propertyName,  
      address:       data.address,  
      type:          data.type,  
      numberOfRooms: parseInt(data.numberOfRooms),  
      monthlyRent:   parseFloat(data.monthlyRent),  
      isOccupied:    false,  
      createdAt:     serverTimestamp()  
    });  
    return { success: true, propertyId: ref.id };  
  } catch (err) {  
    return { success: false, error: err.message };  
  }  
}

// Real-time listener for all properties of a landlord  
function subscribeToProperties(landlordId, callback) {  
  const q \= query(  
    collection(db, 'properties'),  
    where('landlordId', '==', landlordId),  
    orderBy('createdAt', 'desc')  
  );  
  return onSnapshot(q, snap \=\> {  
    const list \= snap.docs.map(d \=\> ({ propertyId: d.id, ...d.data() }));  
    callback(list);  
  });  
}

// Update specific fields on a property document  
async function updateProperty(propertyId, updates) {  
  try {  
    await updateDoc(doc(db, 'properties', propertyId), {  
      ...updates,  
      updatedAt: serverTimestamp()  
    });  
    return { success: true };  
  } catch (err) {  
    return { success: false, error: err.message };  
  }  
}

export { addProperty, subscribeToProperties, updateProperty };

**6.2.4 Payment Tracker Module**

The payment tracker module generates all monthly payment records for a tenant from their move-in date to the current month and manages their status updates. The initializePayments function uses Promise.all to write all initial payment records in parallel rather than sequentially, which significantly reduces the setup time for tenants with long tenancies.

// payments.js  
import { db } from './firebase-config.js';  
import {  
  doc, setDoc, updateDoc, getDocs, collection,  
  query, where, serverTimestamp  
} from 'firebase/firestore';

// Generate YYYY-MM strings from move-in date to today  
function getMonthRange(moveInDate) {  
  const months \= \[\];  
  let cur \= new Date(moveInDate);  
  cur.setDate(1);  
  const now \= new Date();  
  while (cur \<= now) {  
    const y \= cur.getFullYear();  
    const m \= String(cur.getMonth() \+ 1).padStart(2, '0');  
    months.push(\`${y}-${m}\`);  
    cur.setMonth(cur.getMonth() \+ 1);  
  }  
  return months;  
}

// Create initial 'pending' payment records for a new tenant  
async function initializePayments(landlordId, tenantId, moveInDate) {  
  const months \= getMonthRange(moveInDate);  
  await Promise.all(months.map(month \=\> {  
    const id \= \`${tenantId}\_${month}\`;  
    return setDoc(doc(db, 'payments', id), {  
      landlordId, tenantId, month,  
      status: 'pending', amount: null,  
      paidOn: null, notes: '',  
      createdAt: serverTimestamp()  
    });  
  }));  
}

// Mark a specific month's payment status  
async function updatePayment(tenantId, month, status, amount, notes) {  
  const id \= \`${tenantId}\_${month}\`;  
  try {  
    await updateDoc(doc(db, 'payments', id), {  
      status,  
      amount:    amount ? parseFloat(amount) : null,  
      paidOn:    status \=== 'paid' ? new Date().toISOString() : null,  
      notes:     notes || '',  
      updatedAt: serverTimestamp()  
    });  
    return { success: true };  
  } catch (err) {  
    return { success: false, error: err.message };  
  }  
}

export { getMonthRange, initializePayments, updatePayment };

**6.2.5 AI Clause Explainer Module**

The Gemini API is called directly from client-side JavaScript using the Fetch API. The prompt is structured with explicit constraints to keep the AI's response grounded in the pasted text and prevent it from generating general legal statements. The temperature is set to 0.2 (on a 0-to-1 scale) to make responses more factual and less creative. The maxOutputTokens limit of 256 keeps responses concise. The final prompt design used in production was the result of approximately nine iterations — earlier versions either ignored the constraint to stay within the provided text or produced overly long responses.

// ai-explainer.js

const API\_URL \=  
  'https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/' \+  
  'gemini-1.5-flash:generateContent';

async function explainClause(clauseText, userQuestion, apiKey) {  
  const prompt \= \[  
    'You are a helpful assistant that explains rental agreement clauses',  
    'in plain, simple language for non-lawyers.',  
    '',  
    'STRICT RULES:',  
    '- Only explain what is explicitly written in the clause below.',  
    '- Do not add information not present in the clause.',  
    '- Do not give legal advice or opinions on enforceability.',  
    '- Keep your answer to 3-5 sentences.',  
    '- Use simple, everyday English.',  
    '',  
    'CLAUSE:',  
    clauseText,  
    '',  
    'QUESTION:',  
    userQuestion,  
    '',  
    'EXPLANATION:'  
  \].join('\\n');

  try {  
    const res \= await fetch(\`${API\_URL}?key=${apiKey}\`, {  
      method: 'POST',  
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },  
      body: JSON.stringify({  
        contents: \[{ parts: \[{ text: prompt }\] }\],  
        generationConfig: { temperature: 0.2, maxOutputTokens: 256 }  
      })  
    });  
    if (\!res.ok) throw new Error(\`HTTP ${res.status}\`);  
    const data \= await res.json();  
    const text \= data.candidates\[0\].content.parts\[0\].text;  
    return { success: true, explanation: text };  
  } catch (err) {  
    return { success: false,  
      error: 'Could not reach the AI service. Check your connection.' };  
  }  
}

export { explainClause };

**6.2.6 Firestore Security Rules**

The Firestore security rules are the critical access-control layer of the system. Because there is no custom backend server, these rules are the only thing preventing one landlord from reading or modifying another's data. The rules are evaluated server-side before every read or write operation and cannot be bypassed by client-side code. The rules for RentEase follow a consistent pattern: every read and write on every collection requires the requesting user to be authenticated and the landlordId field on the relevant document to match the requesting user's UID.

// firestore.rules  
rules\_version \= '2';  
service cloud.firestore {  
  match /databases/{database}/documents {

    function isAuth() {  
      return request.auth \!= null;  
    }  
    function owns(landlordId) {  
      return request.auth.uid \== landlordId;  
    }

    // Each landlord can only read/write their own profile  
    match /landlords/{uid} {  
      allow read, write: if isAuth() && owns(uid);  
    }

    // Properties, tenants, agreements, payments, complaints  
    // all follow the same pattern: isAuth \+ owns(landlordId)  
    match /properties/{id} {  
      allow read, update, delete: if isAuth()  
        && owns(resource.data.landlordId);  
      allow create: if isAuth()  
        && owns(request.resource.data.landlordId);  
    }

    match /tenants/{id} {  
      allow read, update, delete: if isAuth()  
        && owns(resource.data.landlordId);  
      allow create: if isAuth()  
        && owns(request.resource.data.landlordId);  
    }

    match /payments/{id} {  
      allow read, update, delete: if isAuth()  
        && owns(resource.data.landlordId);  
      allow create: if isAuth()  
        && owns(request.resource.data.landlordId);  
    }

    match /complaints/{id} {  
      allow read, update, delete: if isAuth()  
        && owns(resource.data.landlordId);  
      allow create: if isAuth()  
        && owns(request.resource.data.landlordId);  
    }  
  }  
}

6.3  Testing Strategy

Testing for RentEase was conducted manually throughout the development period. The team chose manual testing over automated test frameworks such as Jest or Cypress for practical reasons. Setting up an automated testing environment for a Firebase-backed application requires mocking Firebase services or using the Firebase Local Emulator Suite, which would have added significant setup complexity. The team's priority was to deliver working features within the available time. Manual testing was sufficient to catch all significant defects before deployment.

Four types of testing were performed. Functional testing verified that each individual feature produced the correct output for a given input. Integration testing verified that the modules worked correctly together and that data flowed correctly across the Firestore collections. Usability testing used external participants who had not been involved in development to evaluate whether the interface was understandable and usable without explanation. Security testing verified that the Firestore security rules correctly blocked unauthorized access attempts.

6.4  Functional Testing

Functional testing was performed feature by feature as each module was completed. Each feature had a defined set of test cases with specific inputs and expected outputs. A feature was considered complete only when all its test cases passed.
